clue.text: Half of answer covered by forceful political publication

indicators.note: something covered by another sits inside it, wrapped round on both sides

parts.note: a hard push is a forceful one

indicators.note: half of a word keeps only its first part, dropping the rest

parts.note: the first three of its six letters

explanation.surface: A forceful political newsletter hides half of its answers.
explanation.walkthrough: HANSARD is the official printed record of debates in the British Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: The transcript of parliamentary debates is published daily, so it is a political publication.

clue.text: Recently stolen on the base, with all possible speed

parts.note: the foot of something is its base

explanation.surface: A thief flees as fast as possible from the base with fresh loot.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue the first part sits on top of the second.
explanation.definitionFit: To go hotfoot is to rush somewhere in great haste, an idiom for speed.

clue.text: Relative, over-particular about everything initially

indicators.note: one part goes about another, surrounding it

parts.note: nice in its old sense means fussy or precise

indicators.note: initially points to the start of a word, its first letter

explanation.surface: A family member fusses over every little thing.
explanation.definitionFit: A niece is the daughter of one's sibling, a family relation.

clue.text: A quiet spot overlooking a northern museum

parts.note: a mole is a spot on the skin

explanation.surface: A peaceful place with a view over a museum in the north.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'overlooking' puts the first part above the second, so it only fixes the order.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ashmolean in Oxford is Britain's oldest public museum, holding art and archaeology.

clue.text: Entirely where a lift may be going

definitions.text: where a lift may be going
definitions.meaning: second meaning: an elevator's descent to street level

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means completely, and literally it names the descent of an elevator to the bottom floor.

clue.text: Marsh bird from intensely cold north

parts.note: a bitter wind is piercingly cold

explanation.surface: A wading bird flees the freezing northern weather.
explanation.definitionFit: The bittern is a heron-family wader that lives in reedbeds, famous for its booming call.

clue.text: Frank, an agent with a weapon, perhaps

parts.note: an instrument is the agent or means by which something is done

explanation.surface: A man called Frank, a secret agent, is carrying a gun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' poses as a man's name and 'agent' as a spy; both are plain vocabulary.
explanation.definitionFit: A blunt instrument such as a club or cosh is the classic murder weapon of detective stories.

clue.text: Person of great strength beat Italian inside

indicators.note: the part named just before it goes inside the other

parts.note: to tan someone's hide is to beat them
standard abbreviation, as in It. vermouth

explanation.surface: A strongman thrashes an Italian indoors.
explanation.definitionFit: The Titans were giant gods of Greek myth, so a titan is anyone of colossal power.

clue.text: Moving out of island motel that's shabby outside

indicators.note: a shabby building is run down and disordered, so these letters are jumbled
the rearranged part goes outside the other, enclosing it

parts.note: Iona is a small island in the Scottish Hebrides

explanation.surface: A guest checks out of a run-down island motel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moving' reads as leaving, but it is the definition meaning touching.
explanation.definitionFit: A moving scene stirs the feelings, so it is emotional in the sense of affecting.

clue.text: Theatre director visiting new Rye convent

indicators.note: a new version of a word has its letters made over in a fresh order

parts.note: Trevor Nunn, former head of the Royal Shakespeare Company and the National Theatre

explanation.surface: A stage director pays a call on a convent in the town of Rye.
explanation.walkthrough: Rye is a small historic town in Sussex; here it is only letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A nunnery is a community house of nuns, which is what a convent is.

clue.text: Send in the Clowns — those two hum song off-key

indicators.note: singing off-key puts the notes wrong, so these letters come out of order

parts.note: fifteen letters of fodder, used in full

explanation.surface: A pair of performers hum the Sondheim song badly out of tune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Send in the Clowns' looks like the song title, but read as an order it is the circus saying carry on whatever happens.
explanation.definitionFit: Sending on the clowns while trouble brews is the classic showbusiness way of insisting the performance continues regardless.

clue.text: This could be up to one to become more communicative

indicators.note: the answer is what the next words could become, if rearranged

explanation.surface: Something that could be up to one person to make them talk more freely.
explanation.definitionFit: To open out is to drop one's reserve and talk more freely, the idiom for becoming expansive.

clue.text: Tenor has money in annuity scheme

indicators.note: one word has the other, holding it within itself

parts.note: the tenor of a letter is its tone or general drift
tin is old slang for cash

explanation.surface: An opera singer with cash puts it into a pension plan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tenor' looks like a singer, T, but it means tone. 'in annuity scheme' reads as one phrase; 'in' only joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A tontine is a shared fund whose subscribers draw an income, the last survivor taking everything: a kind of annuity.

clue.text: Relish latest of paintings placed in gallery

indicators.note: something placed in another goes inside it

parts.note: the Tate is the London art gallery

indicators.note: the latest of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: An art lover savours the newest paintings hung in a gallery.
explanation.definitionFit: A relish for something is a liking or appetite for it, as is a taste for it.

clue.text: Swell cleaner pocketed an additional amount

indicators.note: something pocketed is tucked away inside

parts.note: a surge is a swelling rush
a char is a cleaning lady, short for charwoman

explanation.surface: A posh cleaner quietly kept some extra money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swell' looks like an adjective for smart; it is the noun for a surge of water.
explanation.definitionFit: A surcharge is an extra charge added to the usual price.

clue.text: Two girls after original of toy of little value

indicators.note: the original of a word is where it starts, its first letter

parts.note: first girl: Ena, a short girl's name

explanation.surface: Two girls squabble over a toy that turns out to be worthless.
explanation.walkthrough: The girls come after the toy's letter despite being written first; 'after' fixes the order.
explanation.definitionFit: Ten a penny is the idiom for something so common it is nearly worthless.

clue.text: Spell out what the voter should do?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: communicate clearly, get a message over
second meaning, punned: mark the ballot paper with an X

explanation.walkthrough: The second half splits as PUT A CROSS, the mark British voters make on the ballot.
explanation.definitionFit: To put something across is to explain it successfully, and on a ballot one puts a cross beside the candidate.

clue.text: Australian brings in good books for binding

indicators.note: to bring something in is to take it inside

parts.note: Strine is a jokey name for Australian English, as said in a broad accent

explanation.surface: An Aussie bookbinder brings in fine books for binding.
explanation.definitionFit: Binding rules are strict and must be obeyed, and stringent means strict or tightly enforced.

clue.text: Likes dancing to include very loud 50's music

indicators.note: letters dancing move about out of their places
the rearranged word takes the other inside it

explanation.surface: A fan likes to dance to noisy 1950s tunes.
explanation.definitionFit: Skiffle was a homemade folk-blues style, played on washboard and tea-chest bass, popular in 1950s Britain.

clue.text: Confidential information about extremely unusual flower

indicators.note: one part goes about another, surrounding it

parts.note: a tip is an inside hint

indicators.note: a word's extremes are its two ends, so only its outer letters stay

explanation.surface: A horticultural insider passes on news of a rare bloom.
explanation.definitionFit: The tulip is a spring bulb whose cup-shaped bloom is one of the best-known garden flowers.

clue.text: Haggard, parking, moved slowly

parts.note: inched along, a little at a time

explanation.surface: A worn-out driver crawls forward looking for a parking space.
explanation.definitionFit: A pinched face is thin and drawn from cold or worry, as a haggard one is.

clue.text: Popular, more robust gas mask

explanation.surface: A sturdier, better-liked respirator for use in a gas attack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gas mask' looks like the wartime kit; read differently it is a mask for breathing in a medicinal gas.
explanation.definitionFit: An inhaler delivers a medicinal vapour through a mouthpiece or mask, so it is a device for taking in gas.

clue.text: I must interrupt fat Scottish landowner

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break into the middle of something

explanation.surface: Someone insists on breaking in on a portly Highland estate owner.
explanation.definitionFit: A laird is the Scots term for the owner of a landed estate.

clue.text: Soiled article found by relative

explanation.surface: A dirty item turns up beside a family member.
explanation.definitionFit: Something soiled has been made dirty, which is to say it is not clean.

clue.text: English girl in musical

parts.note: Vita, as in the writer Vita Sackville-West

explanation.surface: An English girl appears in a stage show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a container signal but only joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Evita is the Lloyd Webber and Rice stage show about Eva Perón.

clue.text: Beeswax? Ruin most of upholstery, if badly applied

indicators.note: most of a word is all but its last letter
something applied badly is put on in a mess, so these letters land in the wrong order

explanation.surface: A warning that clumsy application of beeswax will damage the soft furnishings.
explanation.definitionFit: Beeswax is one traditional wood polish rubbed into tables and chairs; the question mark marks it as an example.

clue.text: Rectified awful deed involving servants

indicators.note: something awful is badly done, so these letters are in poor order
to involve something is to take it inside

parts.note: a lord's men are his servants

explanation.surface: A wrong done by household staff has been put right.
explanation.definitionFit: To emend a text is to correct its errors, so emended means corrected or rectified.

clue.text: Modeller, American, caught in a dust storm

indicators.note: a storm whirls things about, so these letters are scattered
something caught in another is trapped inside it

explanation.surface: A US citizen is caught up in a dust storm.
explanation.definitionFit: Marie Tussaud sculpted wax likenesses of famous people, founding the London waxworks that bears her name.
